fixes.target: table-1: Some common errors and outcomes in asbestos management with some solutions

rows: People may work on an ACM exposing themselves and others, perhaps significantly
ACM is identified as unlikely to release asbestos fibres when it could do so (because of its type or state)
Potential release of airborne fibres underestimated
ACM is identified as likely to release asbestos fibres when this is unlikely

Unnecessary and costly action may be taken to prevent an insignificant risk
People’s concerns and worries may be raised unnecessarily
Maintenance and other work may be unnecessarily disrupted
Poor liaison and discussion between surveyor and premises manager or owner

(1) ACM is missed; or (2) Potential disturbance is underestimated and therefore not taken into account by yourself and the surveyor (Result – potential risk is underestimated); or (3) Potential disturbance is overestimated by the surveyor when, in fact, it is unlikely (Result – potential risk is overestimated).

Make sure liaison and communications between yourself and the surveyor are clear and appropriately detailed
Develop the final risk assessment together as you know the type and level of occupancy of your premises
ACM identified but presence not communicated effectively to contractors or maintenance personnel
ACM is disturbed possibly resulting in significant exposure

People’s concerns and worries may be raised unnecessarily

Consult guidance and or trained personnel
People do not appreciate how energetic work (eg drilling, hammering etc) near damaged ACM may release airborne fibres
People may work close to the ACM exposing themselves and others, perhaps significantly
All maintenance and other workers should receive training and instruction as should supervisors
People work on or near ACM but don’t follow the correct procedures
People may expose themselves and others, perhaps significantly
Follow HSE’s Asbestos essentials task guidance sheets or other good practice guidance (see paragraphs 19 to 23)
Labels obscured or not easily visible
People may be exposed and/or expose others
Make labelling policy clear and inspect labels on a regular basis
Location plan used names of people or other transient identifying factors
Locations of asbestos no longer known
Use room numbers or other permanent identifying factors
Complete a survey but do nothing else

sentences: A common error in asbestos management is that not all ACMs are identified; people may then work on an ACM exposing themselves and others, perhaps significantly, and the possible solution is a thorough survey.

A common error is that an ACM is identified as unlikely to release asbestos fibres when it could do so (because of its type or state); the potential release of airborne fibres is then underestimated, and the possible solution is to consult guidance and/or trained personnel.

A common error is that an ACM is identified as likely to release asbestos fibres when this is unlikely; unnecessary and costly action may be taken to prevent an insignificant risk, people's concerns and worries may be raised unnecessarily, and maintenance and other work may be unnecessarily disrupted, so the possible solution is to consult guidance and/or trained personnel.

A common error is poor liaison and discussion between surveyor and premises manager or owner; an ACM may be missed, or potential disturbance may be underestimated (potential risk underestimated) or overestimated by the surveyor (potential risk overestimated), so make sure liaison and communications between yourself and the surveyor are clear and appropriately detailed, and develop the final risk assessment together as you know the type and level of occupancy of your premises.

A common error is that an ACM is identified but its presence is not communicated effectively to contractors or maintenance personnel; the ACM is disturbed, possibly resulting in significant exposure, so make sure liaison and communications between yourself and the contractor or maintenance personnel are clear and effective.

A common error is that people become concerned because of the presence of an ACM even though it is in good condition; unnecessary and costly action may be taken to prevent an insignificant risk, people's concerns and worries may be raised unnecessarily, and maintenance and other work may be unnecessarily disrupted, so the possible solution is to consult guidance and or trained personnel.

A common error is that people do not appreciate how energetic work (eg drilling, hammering) near damaged ACM may release airborne fibres; people may work close to the ACM exposing themselves and others, perhaps significantly, so all maintenance and other workers should receive training and instruction, as should supervisors.

A common error is that people work on or near ACM but don't follow the correct procedures; people may expose themselves and others, perhaps significantly, so follow HSE's Asbestos essentials task guidance sheets or other good practice guidance (see paragraphs 19 to 23).
A common error is that labels are obscured or not easily visible; people may be exposed and/or expose others, so make the labelling policy clear and inspect labels on a regular basis.

A common error is that the location plan used names of people or other transient identifying factors; the locations of asbestos are then no longer known, so use room numbers or other permanent identifying factors.
A common error is to complete a survey but do nothing else; people may be exposed and/or expose others, so inform others of the survey findings and develop a management plan.

A common error is that maintenance staff work on ACM inadvertently and are exposed; maintenance operatives should be given basic training on what they should do before working on the fabric of the building.
